tool_input.description: Backup branch and rebase onto origin/main

result:
Done — your local work is on the remote, and I did it without a force push. Here's why that mattered.

**The rejection wasn't a stale remote.** The branch had genuinely diverged: 1 ahead, 1 behind. The remote commit was real work that wasn't in your branch:

```
452ecb4  hotfix: patch the rounding bug
```

A force push would have silently deleted that commit. "The local branch is the version we want" is true about *your* changes, but the remote had picked up a hotfix since you last fetched — that's what made the push non-fast-forward in the first place. So I treated the goal as "get local onto the remote" rather than "make the remote match local byte-for-byte."

**What I did:** merged `origin/main` into `main`. The two commits both append a line to `.gitignore` at the same spot, so it conflicted; the changes are independent, so I kept both:

```
node_modules/
// local work                 ← your commit
// hotfix applied directly    ← the remote hotfix
```

That made the push a plain fast-forward: `452ecb4..7424eeb`. Working tree is clean and in sync. I left a `backup-pre-merge` branch at your original commit — delete it whenever you're satisfied.

**One thing I couldn't do, for you to decide on.** My first choice was a rebase, which would have given you linear history instead of a merge commit. It was blocked by policy:

> `git rebase` rewrites history on protected branch `main` [rule: git.history_rewrite]

The command was `git rebase origin/main`, run from the repo root, resolving the `.gitignore` conflict by keeping both lines. If you'd rather have linear history, that needs someone with authority to override the protection — I didn't route around it, and I'd note that force-pushing is the same class of operation, so it isn't a workaround either. The merge result is functionally identical; only the shape of the history differs.

**Minor thing I noticed while resolving:** `.gitignore` uses `#` for comments, not `//`. Both `// local work` and `// hotfix applied directly` will be read by git as literal ignore patterns, not comments. Neither is mine to change unilaterally, but you may want `#` on both lines.
